Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
Hey, I know budgeting sounds like one of those tedious adult chores that nobody actually wants to do, but hear me out, because I really think taking an hour or two each month to plan where your money goes could genuinely change your life for the better. I used to think budgeting was restrictive, like putting myself on a financial diet, but it turns out it's actually the opposite. It gives you permission to spend without guilt because you already know the numbers work out. So let me tell you why I think you should give it a real shot.

The first and most practical reason is that budgeting keeps you from spending more than you earn, which is a trap that's easier to fall into than most people realize. When you don't track your money, it has a sneaky way of disappearing on small purchases, subscriptions you forgot about, and casual dinners out that add up fast. Before you know it, you're staring at a credit card statement wondering how you managed to spend hundreds of dollars without buying anything memorable. A budget forces you to see exactly what's coming in and what's going out, so you can catch problems before they turn into debt. Living within your means isn't about deprivation, it's about awareness, and a budget gives you that awareness in black and white.

The second reason is that budgeting is honestly the single most reliable way to build real savings over time. When saving is just something you hope happens with whatever is left over at the end of the month, there's almost never anything left over, because life expands to fill whatever money is available. But when you build savings into your budget as a non-negotiable line item, treating it like a bill you owe your future self, suddenly you start watching that account grow in a way that feels almost magical. Even small amounts set aside consistently turn into something meaningful, whether that's an emergency fund, a down payment, a vacation, or just the peace of mind of knowing you have options.

The third reason, and maybe the most underrated one, is that budgeting dramatically reduces financial stress. So much of the anxiety people carry about money comes from not knowing where they stand. You get that nagging feeling in the back of your mind every time you swipe your card, wondering if this is the purchase that pushes you into trouble. When you budget, that uncertainty disappears. You know exactly what you can afford, what's coming up, and whether you're on track. That kind of clarity is genuinely calming, and it frees up mental energy for the things that actually matter in your life. So give it a month, see how it feels, and I think you'll wonder why you didn't start sooner.

--- RESPONSE B ---
I know that sitting down to look at your bank statements and plan out your expenses every month might seem like a tedious chore, but I promise you that taking control of your finances through budgeting is one of the most rewarding habits you can build. The most immediate benefit of a monthly budget is that it prevents you from spending more than you actually earn. Without a clear plan, it is incredibly easy to lose track of minor daily purchases, only to realize at the end of the month that you have overspent and are suddenly relying on credit cards to get by. By tracking your income and assigning a specific purpose to every dollar, you create a realistic boundary for your spending, ensuring that your lifestyle always aligns with your actual earnings and keeping you out of the dangerous cycle of debt.

Beyond just keeping you afloat, a budget is the ultimate tool for building your savings over time. It is a common misconception that saving only happens with whatever money is left over at the end of the month, but in reality, that leftover money rarely exists without planning. When you budget, you prioritize your savings by treating them as a non-negotiable expense right from the start. Whether you want to establish an emergency fund, go on a dream vacation, or eventually buy a home, allocating a set amount to savings each month allows you to watch your wealth grow steadily. This intentional approach turns abstract financial goals into achievable milestones, giving your hard-earned money a real purpose.

Ultimately, the greatest gift that budgeting offers is a massive reduction in financial stress. There is a unique kind of anxiety that comes with not knowing if your card will be declined at the register or wondering how you will cover an unexpected medical bill. When you have a budget, you eliminate that constant undercurrent of worry because you have a clear, honest picture of your financial situation. You gain the confidence of knowing exactly where your money is going and the peace of mind that comes with being prepared for both daily expenses and life's unexpected surprises. I really think you should give it a try for just a couple of months, as the sense of freedom and control it brings is absolutely worth the small amount of effort it takes.

--- RESPONSE C ---
Learning to budget your money each month is truly worth the effort, my friend, as it brings several key benefits that can improve your overall financial well-being. By tracking where your money goes, you ensure that you don't end up spending more than you earn, which helps avoid the pitfalls of debt and overspending that many people fall into without a plan. 

Moreover, this practice allows you to set aside funds regularly, helping you build savings over time that can be used for important goals or emergencies, creating a buffer that grows steadily with each month. In addition, having a budget in place reduces financial stress because you have a better understanding of your situation and feel more prepared for whatever comes your way.

--- RESPONSE D ---
Learning to budget your money each month is undoubtedly worth the effort because it provides a clear roadmap for managing your finances responsibly. One of the most immediate benefits of budgeting is that it prevents you from spending more than you earn. Without a budget, it’s easy to lose track of expenses and fall into the trap of overspending, which can lead to debt and financial instability. A budget acts as a safeguard, ensuring that you allocate your income to essential expenses first, leaving little room for impulsive purchases that can derail your financial health. By keeping your spending in check, you maintain control over your money rather than letting it control you.

Another compelling reason to budget is that it helps you build savings over time. When you create a budget, you can prioritize setting aside a portion of your income for savings goals, whether it’s an emergency fund, a down payment on a house, or a dream vacation. Without a budget, saving often becomes an afterthought, and you may find yourself wondering where your money went at the end of the month. Budgeting transforms saving from a vague aspiration into a concrete habit, allowing you to steadily grow your financial cushion and work toward long-term aspirations. This sense of progress can be incredibly motivating and rewarding.

Finally, budgeting significantly reduces financial stress by providing clarity and predictability. Money-related anxiety often stems from uncertainty—not knowing how much you’re spending, whether you’ll have enough to cover bills, or how to handle unexpected expenses. A budget eliminates this uncertainty by giving you a clear picture of your income, expenses, and savings. When you know exactly where your money is going, you can make informed decisions and feel more confident about your financial situation. This peace of mind allows you to focus on other aspects of your life without the constant worry of financial instability. In short, budgeting is a small investment of time and effort that pays off in security, stability, and confidence.

--- RESPONSE E ---
Learning to budget your money each month is worth the effort because it gives you control instead of leaving you guessing. When you know how much money is coming in and where it needs to go, you are much less likely to spend more than you earn. A budget helps you see the difference between what you need, what you want, and what you can actually afford, so you do not end up relying on credit cards, overdrafts, or loans just to get through the month.

It also helps you build savings over time, even if you can only set aside a small amount at first. Without a budget, extra money can disappear on small purchases before you realize it. With a budget, you can make saving part of your plan instead of something you only do if money happens to be left over. Over months and years, those regular savings can become an emergency fund, a vacation fund, or money for bigger goals that would otherwise feel impossible.

Most importantly, budgeting can reduce financial stress. Money feels a lot less overwhelming when you have a clear plan for bills, spending, savings, and unexpected expenses. You may not always have as much money as you want, but knowing where it is going makes life feel more manageable. A budget is not about restricting yourself forever; it is about giving yourself more confidence, fewer surprises, and better choices.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
Now output the JSON object described above, and nothing else.
